gloss: (interrogative) is it…?, does…?; (הֲלֹא) is it not…?, surely; (הֲ…אִם) … or …?; whether; the; (with time words) this, today; (addressing) O …!; (on a participle or verb) who, which
summary:
הֲ turns a statement into a question. Prefixed to the first word of a clause, it asks for yes or no ("Is there a word from Yahweh?" "There is", Jer 37:17), and as often asks what the speaker takes to be plain already: with לֹא, הֲלֹא "is it not…?" expects yes ("Did we not cast three men?" "True, O king", Dan 3:24), and without it the question can expect no ("Is anything too wonderful for Yahweh?", Gen 18:14; "Is Yahweh's hand shortened?", Num 11:23); with a following אִם it asks "… or …?", and after verbs of seeing, knowing and testing it means "whether" (Deu 8:2). It is a single syllable with no verb or noun behind it: the same particle is Arabic ʾa- (with ʾ for h, as Arabic also says hayā for ʾayā) and hal, and the הֲ of Daniel's and the Targums' Aramaic, while Ugaritic and Punic mark a yes-no question with no particle at all; so the entry is keyed by its own letter. It is not the article הַ, which doubles the next consonant and stands on nouns and words used as nouns, and which Aramaic lacks (its article is the suffix -ā) though it has this הֲ; that both grew from one pointing h- (as in הֵן, הִנֵּה) is possible, but nothing in the evidence shows it.

הַ is the article "the": one syllable, ha-, prefixed to a noun and doubling its first letter (הַשָּׁמַיִם, הַבַּיִת; before א, ע, ר and often ה, ח, which cannot be doubled, הָ or הֶ). It points out the thing as one the hearer can identify: one already named ("a ram … and Abraham took the ram", Gen 22:13), the only one there is ("the sun had risen on the earth", Gen 19:23), the kind as a whole ("man does not live by bread alone", Deu 8:3), the person spoken to ("Help, O king!", 2Sa 14:4), the present time (הַיּוֹם "today", Exo 14:13), and, on a participle or verb, "the one who" ("to Yahweh who had appeared to him", Gen 12:7). An adjective or pointing word with a definite noun takes it too (הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה "this day", Lev 23:14), but a personal name, a construct noun and a noun with a suffix never do: they are definite already (אֲרוֹן בְּרִית־יְהוָה, Num 10:33). It is a pointing word with no verb or noun behind it, the same as Phoenician and Moabite h-; whether it was once *han- and is akin to the h- of הֵן, הִנֵּה is argued but not shown, so the entry is keyed by its letter. It is not the interrogative הֲ (ha-interrogative), and the Aramaic of scripture has no such prefix: Aramaic makes a noun definite with the ending -ā (מַלְכָּא "the king").

words.gloss: is it…?, does…?; (הֲלֹא) is it not…?; (הֲ…אִם) … or …?; whether
words.summary: About 744 uses in the Hebrew (273 of them הֲלֹא), always joined to the first word of its clause: הֲ before most letters (הֲשֹׁמֵר, Gen 4:9), הַ before a guttural or a shewa (הַאַתָּה, Gen 27:21; הַלְּבֶן, Gen 17:17), הֶ before a guttural with qamets (הֶאָנֹכִי, Num 11:12). Once it stands alone: הֲ לַיהוָה, Deu 32:6. A question can also be asked with no particle at all ("you are my son Esau?", Gen 27:24, after הַאַתָּה in 27:21), so הֲ marks a question but is not needed for one.

senses.gloss: is it…?, does…? (asking yes or no)
senses.definition: Asks whether a thing is so, and is answered yes or no, often by repeating the word asked about ("Is there…?" "There is"; "Is it you?" "I am").

evidence.note: Zedekiah: "הֲיֵשׁ, is there a word from Yahweh?" Jeremiah: "יֵשׁ, there is."
"הַאֶפְרָתִי אַתָּה, are you an Ephraimite?" and he said "No".
"הֲשָׁלוֹם לוֹ, is it well with him?" They said "Well".
"הַאַתָּה זֶה אֲדֹנִי אֵלִיָּהוּ, is it you, my lord Elijah?" and he said "I am" (18:8).
The brothers report Joseph's questions: "Is your father yet alive? Have you a brother?", הַעוֹד … הֲיֵשׁ.
"Are you the man who spoke to the woman?" "I am."
"Is there room in your father's house for us to lodge?"
"הֲשָׁלוֹם, is it peace, Jehu?" answered with another question: "What peace, so long as…?"
"Son of man, הֲתִחְיֶינָה, can these bones live?" A real question; the prophet answers "O Lord Yahweh, you know."
Yahweh to Adam: "הֲמִן הָעֵץ, have you eaten of the tree I commanded you not to eat of?"

senses.gloss: (הֲלֹא) is it not…?, surely; (pointing to a known fact)
senses.definition: With the negative לֹא the question expects the answer yes and calls on the hearer to grant what is plain: "is it not so?", in effect "surely". It points to what is written, seen or known, and can stand where a statement would.

evidence.note: The Aramaic: "הֲלָא, did we not cast three men bound into the fire?" They answered "True (יַצִּיבָא), O king."
"הֲלָא, did you not sign a decree…?" The king answered "The thing is certain."
"הֲלוֹא הוּא אָבִיךָ, is he not your father who bought you?" followed by statements: "he made you and established you".
"הֲלוֹא הֵם כְּתֻבִים, are they not written in the book of the acts of Solomon?": a reference to the record, "they are written".
Jonathan's agreed signal: "הֲלוֹא, is not the arrow beyond you?", meaning "the arrow is beyond you" (20:22).
Four times: "Have you not known? Have you not heard? …"
"Have we not all one father? Has not one God created us?"
Miriam and Aaron: "Has Yahweh spoken only by Moses? הֲלֹא, has he not spoken also by us?": the first expects no, the second yes.
The murmuring at Kadesh: "הֲלוֹא, would it not be better for us to return to Egypt?"
The donkey: "הֲלוֹא, am I not your donkey, on which you have ridden…? הַהַסְכֵּן, was I ever wont to do so to you?" and he said "No": the two kinds of question side by side.
Without לֹא but expecting yes: "הֲנִגְלֹה נִגְלֵיתִי, did I not plainly reveal myself to your father's house in Egypt?"
"הֲלוֹא, if you do well, shall there not be a lifting up?"

senses.gloss: is it…? (expecting no: denial, reproach, disbelief)
senses.definition: The question is put so that the only answer is no: to deny a thing ("Am I my brother's keeper?"), to reproach, or, on unbelieving lips, to doubt that God can do what he says. The answer is often given by the speaker or by events.

evidence.note: "הֲיִפָּלֵא, is anything too wonderful for Yahweh?": answered by the birth of Isaac at the set time (Gen 21:1–2).
"הֲיַד יַהְוֶה תִּקְצָר, is Yahweh's hand shortened? Now you shall see…": answered by the quail (11:31).
Moses: "הֶאָנֹכִי הָרִיתִי, did I conceive all this people? did I beget them…?": he did not, so he cannot carry them.
Cain: "הֲשֹׁמֵר אָחִי אָנֹכִי, am I my brother's keeper?": a denial.
"הֲצֹאן וּבָקָר, shall flocks and herds be slaughtered for them, to suffice them? or (אִם) shall all the fish of the sea be gathered…?"
"Hear now, you rebels: הֲמִן הַסֶּלַע, shall we bring you water out of this rock?"
"הֲיֵשׁ אֱלוֹהַּ, is there a God beside me?" answered at once: "there is no Rock; I know not any."
"Do two walk together unless they have agreed?"
"הַזְּבָחִים, did you bring me slain beasts and offerings in the wilderness forty years?" Quoted in Acts 7:42 with μή.
"הַלְהָרְגֵנִי, do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" Quoted in Acts 7:28 with μή.
"הֲיֹאמַר חֹמֶר, shall the clay say to its potter, What are you making?" Echoed in Rom 9:20 with μή.
"הֲיִקְבַּע, will a man rob God? Yet you rob me."
"הֲמִמֶּנִּי, is anything too wonderful for me?", Yahweh's answer to Jeremiah's "nothing is too wonderful for you" (32:17).
Unbelief: "הֲיוּכַל אֵל, can God prepare a table in the wilderness?", called testing God (78:18) and not believing in him (78:22).
Yahweh's questions to Job: "הֲבָאתָ, have you entered the springs of the sea?"

senses.gloss: (in astonishment or indignation) what! is it…?
senses.definition: A question that is really an exclamation of astonishment, indignation or scorn, often with an infinitive absolute ("will you indeed reign?") or with מְעַט "is it a small thing…?".

evidence.note: Joseph's brothers: "הֲמָלֹךְ תִּמְלֹךְ עָלֵינוּ, will you indeed reign over us?" and they hated him yet more.
Pharaoh's servants: "הֲטֶרֶם תֵּדַע, do you not yet know that Egypt is destroyed?"
"הַמְעַט מִכֶּם, is it a small thing to you that the God of Israel has separated you…?"
Dathan and Abiram turn it back: "הַמְעַט, is it a small thing that you have brought us up … to kill us in the wilderness?"
Moses to Joshua: "הַמְקַנֵּא אַתָּה לִי, are you jealous for my sake?"
"הֲגַם, will he even force the queen before me in the house?"
The adversary: "הַחִנָּם, does Job fear God for nothing?"

senses.gloss: (הֲ … אִם) … or …?; (הֲ … אִם לֹא) … or not?
senses.definition: With אִם before the second half, the question offers two answers to choose between: "is it this, or that?"; with אִם לֹא or אִם אַיִן, "or not?".

evidence.note: "הֲלָנוּ אַתָּה אִם לְצָרֵינוּ, are you for us, or for our adversaries?"
Massah and Meribah: "הֲיֵשׁ יַהְוֶה בְּקִרְבֵּנוּ אִם אָיִן, is Yahweh among us, or not?": the question by which they tested Yahweh.
"הַאַתָּה זֶה בְּנִי עֵשָׂו אִם לֹא, are you my very son Esau, or not?"
The two halves in parallel: "will you indeed reign over us, אִם, or will you indeed rule over us?"
"הַלְּבֶן, shall a child be born to one a hundred years old? וְאִם, and shall Sarah, ninety years old, bear?"
"Shall I yet again go out to battle … or shall I cease (אִם אֶחְדָּל)?"

senses.definition: After a verb of seeing, knowing, asking or testing, הֲ brings in the question to be found out: "to see whether…", often with אִם לֹא "or not".

evidence.note: Yahweh led Israel forty years in the wilderness "to test you, to know what was in your heart, הֲתִשְׁמֹר מִצְוֹתָו אִם לֹא, whether you would keep his commandments or not".
Noah sent the dove "to see הֲקַלּוּ הַמַּיִם, whether the waters were abated".
The manna: "that I may test them, הֲיֵלֵךְ בְּתוֹרָתִי אִם לֹא, whether they will walk in my law or not".
"Now you shall see הֲיִקְרְךָ דְבָרִי אִם לֹא, whether my word shall come to pass for you or not."
The spies are to see the land "whether they are strong or weak, few or many" (הֶחָזָק … הֲרָפֶה, הַמְעַט … אִם רָב), and so on through 13:20.
"to know הַהִצְלִיחַ יַהְוֶה דַּרְכּוֹ אִם לֹא, whether Yahweh had prospered his way or not".
The nations left "to test Israel by them, whether they will keep the way of Yahweh".
"Know now הַכְּתֹנֶת בִּנְךָ הִוא אִם לֹא, whether it is your son's coat or not."

senses.definition: With a first-person verb it asks for a decision: put to Yahweh or to a prophet, "shall I go?", and answered by a command.

evidence.note: David asked of Yahweh: "הַאֵלֵךְ, shall I go and strike these Philistines?" Yahweh said "Go".
"הַאֶעֱלֶה, shall I go up into any of the cities of Judah?" "Go up."
"Shall I pursue? הַאַשִּׂגֶנּוּ, shall I overtake them?" "Pursue, for you shall surely overtake."
Phinehas asks: "Shall I yet again go out…?" "Go up."
Ahab to the prophets: "הַאֵלֵךְ, shall I go against Ramoth-gilead, or shall I forbear?"
"הַאַכֶּה אַכֶּה, my father, shall I strike them?"

greek.gloss: (in a question expecting no) surely not…?

evidence.note: Stephen quotes Amo 5:25: "μή, did you offer me slain beasts and sacrifices forty years in the wilderness?"
Quotes Exo 2:14: "μή, do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?"
"μή, shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why have you made me thus?": Isa 45:9.
μή for הַזְּבָחִים.
μή for הַלְהָרְגֵנִי.
μή for הֲיֹאמַר.
μή for הֲיִפָּלֵא.
μή for הֲיַד.
μή for a real question, answered "No".
"ἢ οὐκ, or has not the potter power over the clay…?": the question of Jer 18:6, "הֲכַיּוֹצֵר … לֹא, can I not do with you as this potter?"
οὐκ for הֲלוֹא.
οὐκ for הֲלוֹא, "is he not your father?"

greek.gloss: whether; (in a direct question) is it…?

evidence.note: εἰ, "whether", for הֲקַלּוּ.
εἰ … ἢ οὔ for הַ… אִם לֹא.
εἰ … ἢ οὔ for הֲיֵשׁ … אִם אָיִן.
εἰ, "whether my word shall overtake you".
εἰ in a direct question: "is it you?"
εἰ in a direct question.

phrases.gloss: is it not…?, surely (273 times)

evidence.note: "הֲלֹא, is not the whole land before you?"

phrases.phrase: הֲלֹא הִיא כְתוּבָה / הֲלֹא הֵם כְּתוּבִים עַל סֵפֶר
phrases.gloss: is it not (are they not) written in the book of…?: the record cited

evidence.note: "Is it not written in the book of Jashar?"

phrases.gloss: … or …?; whether … or not
is it (then) that…?, shall we indeed…? (twice)

evidence.note: After Korah: "הַאִם תַּמְנוּ לִגְוֹעַ, shall we all perish utterly?"

phrases.gloss: is it (really) that…?, is it because…? (five times)

evidence.note: "הֲכִי, is he not rightly named Jacob? for he has supplanted me twice."
"Because you are my brother, should you serve me for nothing?"
"הֲכִי יֶשׁ עוֹד, is there yet anyone left of the house of Saul?"

phrases.gloss: is … also…?, will he even…? (eight times)

evidence.note: "הֲגַם שָׁאוּל בַּנְּבִיאִים, is Saul also among the prophets?" (again 10:12; 19:24).
"Lo (הֵן), he struck the rock … הֲגַם, can he give bread also?"

phrases.gloss: (do you) not yet…? (once)
is there…? (twenty times)
is it well?, is it peace? (fourteen times)

evidence.note: "Is it well with you? with your husband? with the child?" "It is well."

phrases.gloss: is … still…? (ten times)

evidence.note: "I am Joseph; הַעוֹד אָבִי חָי, is my father still alive?"

phrases.gloss: is it a small thing…? (nine times)

evidence.note: "הַמְעַט מִכֶּם, is it a small thing for you to weary men, that you will weary my God also?"

phrases.gloss: will you indeed…? (six times)

evidence.note: "הַאַף תִּסְפֶּה, will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?"

phrases.gloss: is it you…?, are you…? (ten times)

parallels.note: The partner of הֲ in a double question: הֲ opens the first half and אִם the second, as Arabic ʾa- … ʾam (see im).

words.summary: The same particle in Daniel's Aramaic, five times, three of them הֲלָא. Its form is Hebrew's, though Aramaic's article is the suffix -ā, not a prefix.

senses.definition: Asks whether a thing is so.

evidence.note: "הַצְדָּא, is it true, Shadrach, Meshach and Abed-nego, that you do not serve my gods?": answered in 3:16–18.
"Daniel, servant of the living God, הַיְכִל, has your God been able to deliver you from the lions?" Daniel answers "My God sent his angel" (6:23).

senses.definition: With the negative לָא, expects the answer yes.

evidence.note: "Did we not cast three men bound into the fire?" "True, O king."
"Did you not sign a decree…?" "The thing is certain."
"הֲלָא, is not this great Babylon that I have built…?": a boast, not a request for an answer.

words.summary: Written הַ with the next letter doubled, הָ before א, ע, ר (and some ה, ח), הֶ before an unaccented הָ or עָ and before חָ. After the prepositions בְּ, לְ, כְּ the ה drops and its vowel passes to the preposition (בַּבַּיִת "in the house", לַמֶּלֶךְ, כַּשֶּׁלֶג); it is written out only 23 times (כְּהַיּוֹם Gen 39:11; בְּהַשָּׁמַיִם Psa 36:6, English 36:5; בְּהַדֶּרֶךְ Neh 9:19), but kept after מִן (מֵהָאָרֶץ). About 30,200 Old Testament tokens: some 23,800 written with ה and 6,400 hidden in a preposition's vowel.

senses.gloss: the (one named, or known to the hearer)
senses.definition: Marks a thing as one the hearer can already identify: named just before, in view, or known from the situation. A thing is often brought in without it and then taken up with it.

evidence.note: "Let there be אוֹר, light"; then (Gen 1:4) "God saw הָאוֹר, the light, that it was good": first mention without the article, the next with it.
"behold, אַיִל, a ram … and Abraham went and took הָאַיִל, the ram."

"Behold הָאֵשׁ וְהָעֵצִים, the fire and the wood", which they had brought (22:6); "but where is הַשֶּׂה, the lamb?", the one an offering needs. Abraham answers, "God will provide himself הַשֶּׂה, the lamb" (22:8).
"You shall bring עֹמֶר, a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest, to the priest"; then (23:11) "he shall wave הָעֹמֶר, the sheaf".
"Make two silver trumpets"; thereafter בַּחֲצֹצְרוֹת, "with the trumpets" (10:8, 9, 10), the article in the preposition's vowel.
"We are journeying אֶל־הַמָּקוֹם, to the place of which Yahweh said, I will give it you": known by the promise.
"When הָאָרֹן, the ark, set out": the one ark of 10:33.

senses.definition: Marks what exists once in the hearer's world, so that naming it identifies it: the heavens, the earth, the sun, the moon, the sea; and a single office, the high priest, the king of the land.

evidence.note: "God created אֵת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְאֵת הָאָרֶץ, the heavens and the earth."
"הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ, the sun, had risen on הָאָרֶץ, the earth, when Lot came to Zoar."
"הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ וְהַיָּרֵחַ, the sun and the moon, and eleven stars": the stars, many, have no article.
"until the death of הַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדֹל, the high priest".
"הַכֹּהֵן, the priest, shall wave them": whichever priest serves, known by his office.

senses.gloss: the (kind as a whole); (in comparisons) as …
senses.definition: Marks a noun as standing for its whole kind, or any one of it, not a particular one. Comparisons with כְּ "as" usually take it (כַּשֶּׁלֶג "as snow"). English often leaves the article out here, and so does the New Testament's Greek.

evidence.note: "לֹא עַל־הַלֶּחֶם לְבַדּוֹ יִחְיֶה הָאָדָם, man does not live by bread alone": bread and man as kinds. Jesus quotes it with no article on either (Mat 4:4).
"As if a man fled from הָאֲרִי, a lion, and הַדֹּב, a bear, met him … and הַנָּחָשׁ, a serpent, bit him": any lion, bear or serpent.
"הָאֲרִי וְאֶת־הַדּוֹב, a lion, or a bear, came and took a lamb".
"they shall be white כַּשֶּׁלֶג, as snow … כַּצֶּמֶר, as wool": the article in כַּ.
"כָּל־הָאֶזְרָח בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, every native in Israel, shall dwell in booths".

senses.definition: Marks a noun as the person or people spoken to, where English says "O king". The one addressed is the most definite of all; a name needs no article ("Joshua", Zec 3:8), but a title or common noun takes it.

evidence.note: The woman of Tekoa "said to הַמֶּלֶךְ, the king … and said, הוֹשִׁעָה הַמֶּלֶךְ, Help, O king!": the same word spoken of and spoken to.
Abner: "As your soul lives, הַמֶּלֶךְ, O king, I do not know."
"I have a secret word for you, הַמֶּלֶךְ, O king."
"Help, my lord, הַמֶּלֶךְ, O king!"
"הַדּוֹר, O generation, you, see the word of Yahweh!"
Aramaic says it with its definite ending: "מַלְכָּא, O king, live for ever", as Hebrew says "Let my lord הַמֶּלֶךְ David live for ever" (1Ki 1:31).
The Aramaic ṭalyĕthā, with its definite ending, addressing the girl, is given in Greek as τὸ κοράσιον, "the girl", with the article, meaning "girl!".
"Αββα ὁ πατήρ": the Aramaic ʾabbā, addressing the Father, given with the Greek article.

senses.gloss: this (present): הַיּוֹם today, הַפַּעַם this time, הַלַּיְלָה tonight, הַשָּׁנָה this year
senses.definition: On a word of time, marks the one the speaker is in, so that it means "this": the day is "today", the time "this time", the night "tonight". This pointing "this" is the article's force at its plainest.

evidence.note: "see the salvation of Yahweh which he will work for you הַיּוֹם, today; for the Egyptians whom you have seen הַיּוֹם, today, you shall never see again".
Cain: "Behold, you have driven me out הַיּוֹם, this day, from the face of the ground."
"See, I have set before you הַיּוֹם, today, life and good, death and evil."
"הַיּוֹם, today, if you will hear his voice": Hebrews reads it as "σήμερον, today" and presses the word: "exhort one another daily, while it is called today" (Heb 3:7, 13, 15; 4:7).
"זֹאת הַפַּעַם, this at last, this time, is bone of my bones."
"Now let me die, הַפַּעַם, this time, since I have seen your face."
Pharaoh: "I have sinned הַפַּעַם, this time."
"the men who came to you הַלַּיְלָה, tonight".
"he shall lie with you הַלַּיְלָה, tonight".
To Hananiah: "הַשָּׁנָה, this year, you shall die"; and he died "in the same year" (28:17).

senses.gloss: who, which, the one who (on a participle; rarely on a perfect)
senses.definition: On a participle, makes it a relative clause, "the one who does": a description that identifies, like a clause with אֲשֶׁר. In a few places (17 tokens, mostly late books) it stands in the same way on a perfect verb, "who did".

evidence.note: "he built an altar to Yahweh הַנִּרְאֶה אֵלָיו, who had appeared to him".
Yahweh "הַמּוֹלִיכְךָ, who led you through the great and terrible wilderness … הַמּוֹצִיא, who brought you water out of the flint rock, הַמַּאֲכִלְךָ, who fed you manna" (8:15–16).
"הַסֹּלֵחַ, who forgives all your iniquities, הָרֹפֵא, who heals all your diseases, הַגּוֹאֵל, who redeems your life from the pit" (103:3–4).
"הַיֹּשֵׁב, he who sits on the circle of the earth … הַנּוֹטֶה, who stretches out the heavens".
"against הַצַּר הַצֹּרֵר אֶתְכֶם, the adversary who oppresses you".
"הַמַּחֲנוֹת הַחֹנִים קֵדְמָה, the camps that lie on the east".
"Who is the man הַלָּזֶה הַהֹלֵךְ, this one who is walking in the field?"
On a perfect: Yahweh, "הַנִּרְאָה אֵלָיו פַּעֲמָיִם, who had appeared to him twice".
On a perfect: "Ruth the Moabitess … הַשָּׁבָה, who returned from the country of Moab" (so Rut 2:6; 4:3).
"the son of the foreigner הַנִּלְוָה, who has joined himself to Yahweh".
On a perfect: "the men of war הֶהָלְכוּא אִתּוֹ, who went with him".
On a perfect: "Hezekiah rejoiced … because of הַהֵכִין הָאֱלֹהִים, what God had prepared for the people".

senses.gloss: the (repeated on an adjective, ordinal or pointing word: הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה this day)
senses.definition: An adjective, ordinal number, demonstrative or pronoun that describes a definite noun takes the article too, so that "the great light" is הַמָּאוֹר הַגָּדֹל, "this day" הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה, and "that soul" הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִוא, with the pronoun הוּא as "that". An adjective without it, after a definite noun, is said of the noun: "the day is great". An ordinal sometimes takes it alone, as in "the sixth day" (Gen 1:31).

evidence.note: "הַמָּאוֹר הַגָּדֹל, the great light, to rule the day, and הַמָּאוֹר הַקָּטֹן, the lesser light, to rule the night".
"עוֹד הַיּוֹם גָּדוֹל, the day is yet high": the adjective without the article is what is said of the noun.
"until עֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה, this selfsame day".
"I will destroy הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַהִוא, that soul, from among its people": the pronoun with the article is "that".
"הַטּוֹב הַהוּא, that good which Yahweh shall do to us".
"בַּשָּׁנָה הַשֵּׁנִית בַּחֹדֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִי, in the second year, in the second month".
"on the fifteenth day לַחֹדֶשׁ הַזֶּה, of this month".
"יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי, the sixth day", and "יוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי, the seventh day" (Gen 2:3), while the first five are counted without it: "יוֹם אֶחָד, one day" (1:5), "יוֹם שֵׁנִי, a second day" (1:8).
"Ruth הַמּוֹאֲבִיָּה, the Moabitess": a name without the article, its description with it.

senses.gloss: (not used) on personal names, construct nouns and nouns with a suffix
senses.definition: A personal name, a noun bound to a following noun (the construct), and a noun with a pronoun suffix are definite without the article and never take it. A construct chain is definite when its last word is: a name, a suffixed noun, or a noun with the article (מִשְׁכַּן הָעֵדֻת "the tabernacle of the testimony"). אָדָם with the article is "the man"; without it, it becomes the name Adam.

evidence.note: "וַאֲרוֹן בְּרִית־יְהוָה, and the ark of the covenant of Yahweh, went before them": definite through the name, no article. So "עֲנַן יְהוָה, the cloud of Yahweh" (10:34).
"הֶעָנָן, the cloud, was taken up from over מִשְׁכַּן הָעֵדֻת, the tabernacle of the testimony": the article on the last word only.
"יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים, the day of coverings".
"אֶל־פֶּתַח אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד, to the door of the tent of meeting": a chain used as a name, definite with no article at all.
"Yahweh God formed הָאָדָם, the man, of dust"; but "Adam knew his wife again" (4:25) and "the book of the generations of אָדָם, Adam" (5:1), with no article, as a name.
"אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֵן, Aaron the priest": the name bare, the title with the article.
"between זַרְעֲךָ, your seed, and זַרְעָהּ, her seed": definite by the suffix, with no article.
"ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος" for Isa 7:14 "הִנֵּה הָעַלְמָה": the article kept.
"οὐκ ἐπ᾽ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ἄνθρωπος" for Deu 8:3 "עַל־הַלֶּחֶם … הָאָדָם": the generic article dropped.
"ὁ θεὸς Ἀβραάμ" for Exo 3:6 "אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם": the Greek adds an article where the Hebrew construct is definite without one.
"κύριος ὁ θεὸς ἡμῶν" for Deu 6:4 "יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ": an article for the Hebrew suffix.
"προφήτην, a prophet", without the article, for Deu 18:15 "נָבִיא", as the Hebrew.
ἡ for the article of הָעַלְמָה.
ὁ for the article of הָאָדָם; Matthew's Greek drops it.
τῷ ὀφθέντι for הַנִּרְאֶה: article and participle, "who appeared", as the Hebrew.
αἱ παρεμβάλλουσαι for הַחֹנִים.
ἡ ψυχή for הַנֶּפֶשׁ.
ὁ διάβολος for הַשָּׂטָן.
διάβολος with no article for שָׂטָן with none.
βασιλεῦ, the Greek vocative with no article, for the vocative הַמֶּלֶךְ.
θεός with no article for הָאֱלֹהִים: "κύριος ὁ θεός σου, οὗτος θεός ἐστιν".
Quotes Psa 95:7, "הַיּוֹם, today, if you will hear his voice".
"he again marks out a certain day, σήμερον, saying in David, Today".
σήμερον for הַיּוֹם.
σήμερον for הַיּוֹם.

phrases.gloss: today, this day (622 times with the ה written)
this (very) day (177 times, 147 with the ה written)

evidence.note: "הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה, this day, Yahweh your God commands you to do these statutes".
"כְּהַיּוֹם הַזֶּה, about this time", one of the few places the ה is written after כְּ.

phrases.gloss: on this selfsame day: a day fixed exactly (18 times)

evidence.note: Noah enters the ark.
At the end of 430 years, "on this selfsame day all the hosts of Yahweh went out of the land of Egypt".
The day of the firstfruits of wheat, a holy convocation.
The day of coverings: "you shall do no work בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה".
The day Yahweh's hand came on Ezekiel for the vision of the temple.

phrases.gloss: in that day (208 times; 225 with the article written or in the preposition)

evidence.note: "Yahweh alone shall be exalted בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא, in that day".
"בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא, in that day, Yahweh shall be one, and his name one".

phrases.gloss: in the end of the days (13 times): the article on the last word of the chain
this time, now at last (13 times)
the land; the earth (1,024 times with ה written, 258 in a preposition's vowel)

evidence.note: "when you come into הָאָרֶץ, the land, which I give you".

phrases.gloss: the people (859 times, and 96 in a preposition's vowel)
the God, the true God (374 times, and twice in a preposition's vowel)

evidence.note: "וְהָאֱלֹהִים נִסָּה, and God tested Abraham".

phrases.gloss: the priest (576 times with the plural, and 54 in a preposition's vowel); הַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדוֹל the high priest

evidence.note: "יְהוֹשֻׁעַ הַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדוֹל, Joshua the high priest".

phrases.gloss: the king; (addressing him) O king (1,120 times, and 113 in a preposition's vowel)

cognates.gloss: is it…? (the interrogative prefix); with أَمْ, … or …?; with لَمْ, did … not?; after "I know not", whether
cognates.note: The same one-syllable prefix with the same uses: a question answered نَعَمْ "yes" or لَا "no"; أَلَمْ "did we not…?" as הֲלֹא; with أَمْ for the second half of a double question, as הֲ … אִם; to reprove, to deny, to express wonder; and after "I care not" or "I know not", "whether". It has ʾ where Hebrew has h, a correspondence seen in other particles: Arabic says هَيَا for the vocative أَيَا, "ه being substituted for its hemzeh".

evidence.locator: Book I, pp. 1–3, art. ا, أَلِفُ الٱِسْتِفْهَامِ (the interrogative alif)
evidence.note: أَقَامَ زَيْدٌ "Did Zeyd stand?", "to which the answer is لَا or نَعَمْ"; أَزَيْدٌ عِنْدَكَ أَمْ عَمْرٌو "Is Zeyd with thee, or 'Amr?"; أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ "Did we not dilate?"; used to reprove, to deny, to denote wonder; after مَا أُبَالِى, "I care not whether thou stand or sit".

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 135, art. ايا, أَيَا
evidence.note: "ه is substituted for its hemzeh; so that one says, هَيَا."
Introduces a positive or negative yes-no question; with أَمْ an alternative question; derived there from an older ha-, cognate with Hebrew הֲ.

cognates.gloss: is it…? (introducing a yes-no question); with أَمْ, … or …?
cognates.note: Arabic's other yes-no particle, with Hebrew's h. Its -l is taken to be the affirmative la-, so it is not the same compound as הֲלֹא, whose לֹא is "not". Arabic أَمْ can also stand alone "in the sense of هَلْ", as Hebrew uses אִם alone in some questions.

evidence.note: "introduces a positive yes-no question"; "indicates an exclusive disjunction with أَمْ"; analysed as ha- (now ʾa-) + l-.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 3044, art. هل, هَلْ
Book I, p. 88, art. ام, أَمْ
evidence.note: "It is also used as a simple interrogative … in the sense of هَلْ; or in the sense of the interrogative أَ".

cognates.gloss: is it…? (interrogative prefix); הֲלָא is it not?, indeed
cognates.note: The Targums use the same prefix as Daniel, and הֲלָא for Hebrew הֲלֹא, as in Onkelos at Gen 4:7 and 4:9.

evidence.note: "an interrogative prefix. Targ. O. Gen. IV, 9"; "With לא, הֲלָא … is it not?, behold, indeed. Targ. Gen. IV, 7".

cognates.gloss: the (definite article); who, which (on a participle or perfect); O …! (vocative)
cognates.note: The same article with the same uses, one by one: with a noun, with a noun taken generically, on an adjective after a definite noun (ym h-ḥmšy "the fifth day", as Hebrew יוֹם הַשִּׁשִּׁי), on demonstratives in late Punic, introducing a relative clause on a participle and on a perfect (ʾnk ʾztwd h-brk bʿl "I am Azatiwada, whom Baal blessed"), and as a vocative. In Punic it is also written ʾ- and pronounced with the next consonant doubled, as Hebrew; Krahmalkov takes both shapes to come from a West Semitic pointing word *han-.

evidence.locator: pp. 153–154, H- pron. THE (definite article), uses 1–10
evidence.note: KAI 26 A II 9 wbn ʾnk hqrt z "I built this city"; KAI 76 B 1 ym hʾrbʿy "the fourth day"; KAI 26 A I 1 ʾnk ʾztwd hbrk bʿl "I am Aztwadda, whom Baal blessed"; KAI 165 "Tarry, O passer-by".

"The Punic definite article has two, complementary shapes, each a different reflex of the Proto-West Semitic demonstrative *han-": /iC-/ with gemination of the consonant, and /a:-/ before the laryngeals and pharyngeals.
"the"; from Phoenician 𐤄.

cognates.note: Moabite, the closest neighbour of Hebrew, writes the article as Hebrew does, also with a demonstrative after it (הבמת זאת "this high place", as Hebrew הַבָּמָה הַזֹּאת).

evidence.note: Line 3 ואעש הבמת זאת לכמש בקרחה; line 24 ואמר לכל העמ; line 26 ואנכ עשתי המסלת בארנן.
"And I made this high place for Kemôš"; "And I said to all the people"; "I made the high-road by the Arnon."

cognates.gloss: the (particle of determination); (on a participle) who, which
cognates.note: Arabic's article has the Hebrew article's uses almost one for one: a thing known by being mentioned before, or present, or in the mind; اَلْيَوْمَ "this day, today" as הַיּוֹם; the whole species; a title used for the one pre-eminent; with يَا أَيُّهَا in addressing ("O man"); and, before an active or passive participle, "he who" (اَلضَّارِبُ "he who strikes"), and in poetry even before a verb, as Hebrew rarely before a perfect. Its l assimilates to many following consonants, doubling them (اَلرَّجُلُ ar-rajul), as the Hebrew article doubles every consonant it can. But its form does not answer the Hebrew's sound for sound: Arabic has ʾ/l where Hebrew has h and doubling, and some Yemenite dialects say am- for it. Lane also records a rare ʾal used for the interrogative hal, the only hint found of article and question particle sharing a form. So the likeness of use is plain, the shared origin only possible.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 74, art. ال, اَلْ
evidence.note: "a particle of determination … equivalent to our article The"; used "to distinguish a noun as known": by being mentioned before, by being conceived in the mind, by being applied to a thing present ("اَلْيَوْمَ … This day"); "to denote the species"; with يَا أَيُّهَا الرَّجُلُ "O man"; "a conjunct noun in the sense of الَّذِى" before participles; in the dialect of Himyer امْ for ال; أَلْ فَعَلْتَ "in the sense of هَلْ فَعَلْتَ".
"the"; etymology "uncertain".

cognates.gloss: lo!, look! (calling attention); prefixed to the demonstrative in هٰذَا hāḏā "this"
cognates.note: A pointing h- with a vowel a, as the article's, which Arabic prefixes to its demonstrative (hā + ḏā "this"), as Hebrew's article goes before זֶה in הַלָּזֶה. Hebrew's own pointing words with h, הֵן and הִנֵּה "lo", הֵנָּה "hither", are of the same kind. That the article grew from such a word fits its "this" (הַיּוֹם "today") but cannot be shown.

evidence.note: "The هَا, termed تَنْبِيهٌ [calling attention] … When followed by a pronoun, as هو, &c., it is best rendered Lo."
هَا, "to give notice, to a person addressed, of something about to be said to him, is prefixed to ذَا … thus you say هٰذَا".
"Possibly akin to Arabic هَا (hā) and هٰذَا (hāḏā, 'this')"; with an assimilated -n of *han-.

cognates.note: The Aramaic of the Talmud and Targums has a pointing הָא "this" (and "lo!"), and builds "this" as hā + dēn (הָדֵין) as Arabic builds hāḏā. Aramaic never made it a prefixed article: its definite noun ends in -ā. Scripture's Aramaic has הָא only as "lo!" (Dan 3:25), which is not claimed here.

evidence.note: "(demonstr. pronoun) this": Yoma 26a הא שכיחא והא וכ׳ "the one is a frequent performance, but the other is rare".
The Mishnaic Hebrew article "(followed by Dagesh forte) the"; in the Aramaic "= הָא".

cognates.note: Akkadian has no article, but its demonstrative "this" has the n of the proposed *han-, with Akkadian's usual loss of h. If the Hebrew article is *han- with its n assimilated, annû is its kin; if not, it is only a pointing word of like shape. It does not join the article to the pronoun הוּא, whose h Akkadian writes š (šū).

evidence.note: "this, these"; "Compare Aramaic הָ־ (hā-, 'this') and perhaps Biblical Hebrew הַ(נ)־ (ha(n)-, definite article)."

doctrine.statement: Yahweh asks Abraham, "Is anything too wonderful for Yahweh?" (Gen 18:14), a question whose answer is no, and he answers it by deed: Sarah bore a son "at the set time of which God had spoken" (Gen 21:1–2). In the wilderness Moses asks whether flocks and herds, or all the fish of the sea, could suffice the people (Num 11:22); Yahweh answers with the same kind of question, "Is Yahweh's hand shortened? Now you shall see whether my word shall come to pass for you or not" (Num 11:23), and the wind brought the quail (Num 11:31). Israel asked the question the other way: "Is Yahweh among us, or not?" (Exo 17:7) and "Can God prepare a table in the wilderness? … can he give bread also?" (Psa 78:19–20), which the psalm calls testing God and not believing him (Psa 78:18, 22). Jeremiah confesses "nothing is too wonderful for you", and Yahweh puts it back to him as a question (Jer 32:17, 27); Isaiah has "Is my hand shortened at all, that it cannot redeem?" (Isa 50:2). The angel's word to Mary, "no word shall be impossible with God" (Luk 1:37), says as a statement what Gen 18:14 asked. So when Yahweh asks whether he can, the question is put to be believed; when men ask it of him, it is unbelief.

Several of scripture's questions expecting the hearer's assent are about who God is. "Is he not your father who bought you? He made you and established you" (Deu 32:6). "Is there a God beside me? There is no Rock; I know not any" (Isa 44:8), after "I am the first and I am the last, and beside me there is no God" (Isa 44:6). "Have we not all one father? Has not one God created us?" (Mal 2:10). Each question expects yes, or for Isa 44:8 no, and each answer is the same: one God, who is the father who made his people. Paul says it as a statement: "to us there is one God, the Father, of whom are all things" (1Co 8:6).

Ezekiel sets out God's will as a pair of questions: "Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? says the Lord Yahweh; is it not rather that he should turn from his ways and live?" (Ezk 18:23). The first expects no, the second (הֲלוֹא) yes. The chapter states the same plainly, "I have no pleasure in the death of him that dies … turn and live" (Ezk 18:32), and Ezk 33:11 swears it: "as I live, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live; turn, turn … why will you die?" The two outcomes set before the wicked are dying and living: the one who turns "shall surely live, he shall not die" (Ezk 18:28), the one who turns from righteousness "shall die" in his sin (Ezk 18:24). So God's wish is that men should turn and live, and the end of the one who does not turn is death.

With the article, הַשָּׂטָן is "the adversary" of one scene: seventeen times, in Job 1–2 (Job 1:6; 2:1) and Zec 3:1–2, where the verse gives his part in its own words: "and הַשָּׂטָן, the adversary, standing at his right hand לְשִׂטְנוֹ, to oppose him" (Zec 3:1). Without the article שָׂטָן is any opponent, and scripture gives it to men and to Yahweh's own messenger: the angel of Yahweh stood in the way "לְשָׂטָן, for an adversary" to Balaam (Num 22:22, 32); the Philistine lords feared David would become one to them (1Sa 29:4); God raised up Hadad and Rezon as adversaries to Solomon (1Ki 11:14, 23); and "an adversary stood up against Israel and moved David to number Israel" (1Ch 21:1), where the same account says "the anger of Yahweh was kindled against Israel, and he moved David" (2Sa 24:1). Hebrew never puts the article on a personal name: אָדָם is "the man" with it (Gen 2:7) and the name Adam without it (Gen 4:25; 5:1). So הַשָּׂטָן is a description, "the adversary", the one opposing in that scene, and not a proper name.

On Carmel the question was which is הָאֱלֹהִים, "the God": "If Yahweh is הָאֱלֹהִים, follow him; but if הַבַּעַל, follow him" (1Ki 18:21), Baal too with the article, "the master", a title. Elijah set the test: "the God who answers by fire, he is הָאֱלֹהִים" (1Ki 18:24); and when the fire fell, the people said, "Yahweh, he is הָאֱלֹהִים; Yahweh, he is הָאֱלֹהִים" (1Ki 18:39). Moses had said the same: "Yahweh, he is הָאֱלֹהִים; there is none else beside him" (Deu 4:35, 39). The name Yahweh never takes the article; אֱלֹהִים takes it when it means the one who is God in truth, and the confession joins the name to it. Jesus prays to the Father as "the only true God" (Jhn 17:3).

The sign given to Ahaz points at one woman: "הִנֵּה הָעַלְמָה, behold, the young woman, shall conceive and bear a son" (Isa 7:14), with the article, as "behold, the fire and the wood" points at what is in view (Gen 22:7). Matthew keeps the article, "ἰδοὺ ἡ παρθένος", and says the sign was fulfilled when Mary, before she and Joseph came together, was found with child of the holy spirit (Mat 1:18, 22–23). The article shows a particular woman, not any woman; Matthew names her.

Moses' promise has no article: "נָבִיא, a prophet, from your midst, of your brothers, like me, Yahweh your God will raise up" (Deu 18:15, 18). By the time of John the Baptist the people spoke of him with the article, as one known: "Are you ὁ προφήτης, the prophet?" (Jhn 1:21, 25); "this is truly the prophet who comes into the world" (Jhn 6:14; 7:40). Peter, quoting Moses, keeps the Hebrew's "a prophet" (Act 3:22) and says God raised him up in Jesus (Act 3:26). So the article in the Gospels marks the one Moses promised, and the promise itself named no one but described him.

The promises speak of "your seed" and "her seed" (Gen 3:15; 22:18), definite by the suffix, which in Hebrew takes no article. Paul's argument rests on the number, not on an article: "He does not say, and to seeds, as of many, but as of one, and to your seed, which is Christ" (Gal 3:16); and the law was added "until τὸ σπέρμα, the seed, should come to whom the promise was made" (Gal 3:19), the Greek article pointing back to the seed already named in the promise.

(1) Form: one syllable ha- with the next consonant doubled, or, where the consonant cannot be doubled, the vowel lengthened (הָאָרֶץ) or kept short before ה, ח (virtual doubling). Nothing in scripture's Hebrew shows a longer base: no n or l ever appears, not even before a vowel (הָאָדָם, not *הַנְאָדָם or *הַלְאָדָם). No verb or noun הה/הנן/הלל could give "the". (2) The *han- theory: the doubling-or-lengthening pattern is what an assimilated n does in Hebrew (מִן: מִמִּצְרַיִם but מֵאֶרֶץ, exactly as הַמֶּלֶךְ but הָאָרֶץ); Krahmalkov derives the Punic article from a West Semitic demonstrative *han- (pp. 24–25); Akkadian annû "this" has the n; Hebrew's own pointing words הֵן, הִנֵּה, הֵנָּה and Ugaritic hn "behold" (Segert p. 81, §58.1) share h-n; the South Arabian article is a suffixed -n; and the Dedanite/Lihyanite inscriptions are said to write the article h- but hn- before ʾ and ʿ, where Hebrew lengthens (not checked: no Dedanite, Safaitic or Thamudic source is in sources.json). Against it: מָה "what" doubles the next consonant after its shortened vowel (מַה־זֹּאת, Gen 3:13) with no n, so doubling after a short ha- needs no lost consonant; and none of these languages is shown to have had *han- as an article. Evidence: moderate for a pointing h(n)- behind the article; none for a root. (3) The *hal- theory (from Arabic al-) is weaker: Arabic has ʾ, not h; its l is the consonant that assimilates, and some Yemenite dialects say am- (Lane p. 74), so even in Arabic the consonant is not fixed; Hebrew הַלָּז, הַלָּזֶה (in zeh.json) is the article with a pointing l before ז, the same build as Arabic al-la-ḏī, and shows the l as a separate element, not part of the article. (4) Distribution: Ugaritic has no article (Segert p. 51, §52.6: "There is no definite article in Ugaritic"; p. 14, §12.3, a conservative feature); Akkadian has none; Aramaic has a suffixed -ā (the emphatic state), Sabaic a suffixed -n, Arabic prefixed al-, Phoenician, Moabite and Hebrew prefixed h-. Each language built its article late and from its own pointing words, which is why the articles do not answer one another sound for sound. Hebrew's is one of the Canaanite group's (Phoenician, Moabite, Hebrew), and only there is the article strictly cognate. (5) The pronoun הוּא: not the same h. Akkadian writes the pronoun šū with š (hu.json), but its "this", annû, with no š; the article goes with the pointing words, not with the pronoun. The article does combine with the pronoun to make "that" (הַהוּא, Lev 23:30). (6) The interrogative הֲ: not shown to be one word with the article. Lane's rare ʾal for hal (p. 74) is the only hint of a shared form. A common pointing h- behind both, and behind הֵן/הִנֵּה, is possible but nothing shows it; so this entry is homograph 2 and ha-interrogative homograph 1, and no merger is proposed.
